text:
A: Hello, hello, yeah, can you hear me? Tomasz.
B: Hello, yes, I can hear you fine. I'm Alison. Sorry, I'm still getting used to all this.
A: No, it's fine, it's fine. Listen, that puzzle at the start, did you finish it? I think I was fast, I don't know.
B: Oh, erm, I sort of finished it. I wasn't very quick. I kept double-checking. That's me all over really.
A: Ha. I don't check, I just go. So what do you do, Alison?
B: I'm a practice nurse, at a GP surgery in Ipswich. So diabetes reviews, asthma, smears, jabs, that sort of thing.
A: Nurse, okay. My wife, Agnieszka, she's care assistant, in a home, residential. Shifts, nights, everything. Hard job, you know? Paid nothing.
B: Oh, it is hard, that's ever so hard work. I was a healthcare assistant at the hospital before I trained, so I know. Bless her. Does she like it?
A: She likes the old people. She doesn't like the managers. Same like me, I think.
B: (laughs) What do you do, then?
A: Telesales. I sell business energy, water, to small firms, takeaways, garages, salons. On the phone all day. Listen, people think it's easy. It's not easy. You ring a kebab shop at lunchtime, the guy swears at you, puts phone down, you ring the next one. Last month our team hit target and honestly, I carried them. I was top three on the board most of the month.
B: Gosh. I don't think I could do that. I'd be apologising to everyone.
A: That's why you are nurse and I am sales, yeah?
B: That's true. Do people really swear at you?
A: Every day. Doesn't bother me. It's not personal, they don't know me. You just keep going.
B: I suppose that's a good attitude to have, really. I take everything home with me, I'm afraid. I'll lie awake thinking, did I put the right code in.
A: No, no. Home is home. You are Ipswich, yeah? I've never been. For me it's Birmingham Airport, M6, that's my life. Junction 10 is a nightmare every morning.
B: Oh, I've heard about the M6. Ipswich is all right, it's quiet. I walk along the river most days. And I've got a cat, Biscuit. You might have seen his tail in my picture.
A: I saw a bit of orange, yeah. Not a cat man. Dog, maybe. My son wants a dog. He's fifteen, he'll never walk it, he's on PlayStation whole day.
B: (laughs) They all are. My son was the same at fifteen, and now he's got a little girl of his own, so it all comes round. I mind her on Fridays.
A: That's nice. Grandmother, yeah? You don't look it.
B: Oh, stop it. I'm fifty-nine. I'm ever so proud of her, though.
A: And apart from work? You walk, you have cat...
B: I sing in a choir, alto. Tuesday nights in a church hall. We're doing the Christmas concert soon, so it's all carols at the minute.
A: Choir. Okay. I do five-a-side, Thursday. Same idea, you know. You go with people, you shout a bit.
B: Well, we try not to shout! But I suppose, yes, it's sort of the same. It's for the company really.
A: Exactly. Company. And beer after, for us. For you I think tea and biscuit.
B: Tea and biscuits, yes, and I'm meant to be cutting down, so that's going well.
A: Ha. Listen, Ipswich Town, you follow? They went up, yeah? Very good.
B: My dad was a season ticket holder, so I keep half an eye. I was chuffed, I must say. Do you have a team?
A: Lech Poznań, from Poland, and Wolves a bit. Wolves, the referees, honestly, last week —
